analysis:
The PR changes only docs/reference/protocol-messages.md: the 'Last updated' date (line 3) and a new section 'Close codes and the reconnect wait' (head lines 173-190). No executable code, wire format, key handling, authorization or attestation logic changes. The new text documents that the provider reads only the WebSocket close code (not the reason). Code 1012 draws a wait from serviceRestartDelayRange without growing the backoff, and any other code grows the ExponentialBackoff. A session open for stableSessionDuration or more, counted from register, resets the backoff. Every reconnect sends a fresh register.

Security relevance: this touches TB-002 (coordinator-to-provider WebSocket) and, indirectly, availability. The coordinator is trusted, so a close code it sends is not adversarial input. A network attacker able to inject a forged close would need to break TLS, which is outside the scope here. Because the section says the reconnect always sends a fresh register, and the existing doc (lines 94-100) says the resume nonce is fresh per NWConnection, the stated behavior is consistent with the endpoint-resumption and reconnect lifecycle controls (T-053): no old socket state is reused. The documentation does not claim that a close grants or extends authorization.

Unverified contract: the actual behavior of CoordinatorReconnectPolicy.swift, serviceRestartDelayRange and stableSessionDuration is not in the supplied evidence, so I cannot confirm the doc matches the code. That is a documentation-accuracy question, not a security regression. The claim that older providers treat 1012 like any other close is likewise unverified. No threat model update is needed. The doc's edits to existing text appear only as the date change. I found no data exposure, secrets or new attack surface.
